question: Will the Kennedy Center's main building be open to the general public on October 2, 2026?

calls.reasoning: Main building closed since Sept 16 for cited structural safety issues (ceiling collapse, roof canopy); board separately voted for a 2-year renovation closure targeting summer 2028 reopening, and layoffs tied to that plan have begun. Judge Cooper declined to order reopening (only imposed 30-day notice before demolition/major changes); status report due Sept 23 with no indication of a reopening order. Fencing remains up. No market directly prices this contract; demolition markets (11% Kalshi) are a different question. Reopening within the ~10 days remaining before Oct 2 would require both a favorable court ruling AND completed physical remediation - a tight, low-probability path given the parent board's clear long-term closure intent.
calls.dossier:
- Main building physically fenced off and closed to public entry since Sept 16, 2026, per multiple wire reports (AP/ABC News, 2026-09-16/17).
- Cause cited: 'acute risks to public safety' from structural deterioration - partial ceiling collapse and roof-terrace canopy inspection findings, per Executive Director Matt Floca's sworn court declaration (2026-09-17).
- Floca stated closure would last 'seven days, unless extended,' with weekly reevaluation of continued closure (court filing, 2026-09-17).
- Separately, Kennedy Center board of trustees (chaired by Trump) voted Sept 15, 2026 to close the main building for ~2 years for a $257M renovation, with board's own target reopening around summer 2028 (Time, NBC News, PBS, 2026-09-15/16).
- DOJ/Kennedy Center position: the emergency safety closure is legally distinct from the board's 2-year renovation vote and does not violate the standing preliminary injunction against prolonged closure (court filing, 2026-09-17).
- Judge Christopher Cooper (D.D.C.) denied Rep. Joyce Beatty's motion for an emergency hearing to force reopening (2026-09-17/18).
- Cooper ordered 30 days' notice before any demolition or major physical change to the building; this order does NOT compel reopening to the public (Axios, PBS, ABC News, 2026-09-17/18).
- Cooper ordered a detailed status report, with sworn declaration, on the closure and emergency repairs, due 2026-09-23 (multiple sources, 2026-09-17/18).
- Kennedy Center has begun layoffs tied to the broader planned closure, per internal staff email from Floca (AOL/wire reports, 2026-09-18).
- The REACH annex (separate building, does not count for this question's resolution) remains open with scheduled free public events through late September 2026, including Sept 23, 24, and 25 programming (Kennedy Center official site, accessed 2026-09-22).
- No reporting found (through 2026-09-22) of the main building reopening, fencing being removed, or public entry resuming since the Sept 16 closure.
- No reporting found of the Sept 23 status report's content or any subsequent court ruling (report was due the day after the 'Now' timestamp for this forecast).
- Searched for a direct prediction market matching 'will the Kennedy Center main building be open to the public on Oct 2' - none found on Polymarket or Kalshi. Found only adjacent/non-matching contracts: Kalshi 'will the Kennedy Center be demolished this year' (~11% Yes, as of ~2026-09-18) and Polymarket demolition-announcement markets (7-32% Yes across different deadlines) - these price demolition announcements, not physical public-access status, so they are not a resolution-matching anchor.
- Event window per resolution criteria: October 2, 2026 (US Eastern), a single calendar day. As of 'Now' (2026-09-22), 0% of the event window itself has elapsed (window has not begun); roughly 10 days remain between 'Now' and the start of the event window.
- Resolution instrument: official Kennedy Center website hours together with credible reporting on ACTUAL physical access; website-listed hours alone do not control if they conflict with reporting of physical closure (per resolution criteria text).

calls.reasoning: Three independent runs converge tightly (0.07, 0.08, 0.08) with no factual disagreements among them. Two independent closure mechanisms both point NO: (1) a safety-driven closure since Sept 16 citing a real ceiling collapse and roof-canopy risk, framed as 'temporary/7 days' but with fencing still up as of Sept 21-22 and layoffs already underway; (2) the board's separate Sept 15 vote for a ~2-year renovation closure targeting summer 2028 reopening. Judge Cooper declined to compel reopening, only requiring 30-days' notice before demolition/major changes and a Sept 23 status report (whose contents fall after the 'Now' anchor). For Oct 2 to resolve YES, both the safety rationale would need to lift AND the board's independently-voted multi-year closure would need to be reversed or ignored within ~10 days -- an unlikely conjunction given aligned political incentive on the board and no judicial order forcing access. Reference class: emergency safety closures of major public buildings, where the controlling body also independently wants prolonged closure for unrelated reasons, reopening fully within 2-3 weeks without external compulsion is rare (~5-10%). No market directly prices this contract; nearest Polymarket/Kalshi contracts price 'demolition announced' (7-32% across various deadlines), a materially different and more extreme event (an announcement, not physical access status), so not used as a numeric anchor -- though their low near-term values are broadly consistent with no imminent dramatic reversal in either direction.
calls.reconciliation: Listed disagreements among the three runs: none were factual -- all agree on dates (board vote 9/15, closure 9/16, Floca declaration 9/17, status report due 9/23), the dual closure mechanisms, the court's refusal to compel reopening, and lack of any post-9/21 reporting on reopening. Differences were purely emphasis/judgment (Run 2 and 3 weight the 'pretext' narrative and protests slightly more heavily than Run 1), which does not move the needle since all three land in the same narrow 0.07-0.08 band. No web access this run to check for developments after the dossiers' cutoff (Sept 21-22), so reconciliation rests entirely on the converged evidence already gathered. Given the redundancy of two independent closure mechanisms (safety closure AND board's 2-year renovation vote) both needing to reverse within ~10 days for YES, I set the final estimate marginally below the pooled runs at 0.06 rather than averaging to ~0.077, reflecting that the conjunction of reversals required is stricter than any single run's framing captured.
